question: In British Columbia, why is a provincial budget vote normally considered a confidence matter?
generated_answer: You may have heard the expression, “the power of the purse.” That phrase reminds us that the British North America Act of 1867 gives Parliament the power to tax and spend, and that the Executive, represented by the Government, needs Parliament’s approval to spend money. You may also have heard that a budget vote is considered a “confidence” matter. That means that if the House of Commons votes against the budget, the Government has lost the confidence of the House, and the Government is expected to resign. In British Columbia, the provincial budget vote is also a confidence matter. In fact, section 25 of the Constitution Act, 1867 says that “It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill for the Appropriation of any Part of the Public Revenue, or of any Tax or Impost, to any Purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by Message of the Governor General in the Session in which such Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill is proposed.” The message from the Governor General is called a “royal recommendation.” It is an indication that the Governor General has been consulted about the budget, and that the Governor General has agreed to the budget. The royal recommendation is required for all budget bills, including the main estimates, the supplementary estimates, and the budget bill itself. If the House of Commons votes against the budget, the Government is expected to resign. This is because the Government has lost the confidence of the House, and the Government is no longer able to govern. In British Columbia, the provincial budget vote is also a confidence matter. In fact, section 85 of the Constitution Act, 1867 says that “It shall not be lawful for the Legislative Assembly to adopt or pass any Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill for the Appropriation of any Part of the Public Revenue, or of any Tax or Impost, to any Purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by Message of the Lieutenant Governor in the Session in which such Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill is proposed.” The message from the Lieutenant Governor is called a “royal recommendation.” It is an indication that the Lieutenant Governor has been consulted about the budget, and that the Lieutenant Governor has agreed to the budget. The royal recommendation is required for all budget bills, including the main estimates, the supplementary estimates, and the budget bill itself. If the Legislative Assembly votes against the budget, the Government is expected to resign. This is because the Government has lost the confidence of the Legislative Assembly, and the Government is no longer able to govern.
